source: Goyal et al. (2022) Coordination among neural modules through a shared global workspace
finding: Adds a small shared workspace that modules write to by competition and read from by broadcast. Replaces pairwise attention.
numbers: Workspace of nm memory slots, read and write by attention. Cost is near constant in module count, not quadratic. Paper compares the slot count to human working memory (under 10 slots).
limits: Engineered for accuracy, not tested for conscious-like behaviour. The workspace is hidden-state vectors, not text.
agent_relevance: Maps to our design: one small shared state, chosen items written in, all steps read it.

source: Goyal et al. (2022) shared workspace, CATER object tracking
finding: Workspace Transformers match or slightly beat plain Transformers on object tracking.
limits: Gains are about 0.3 to 0.8 points and are close to the error bars for several rows. Not a clear win.
agent_relevance: The accuracy gain from a bottleneck alone is small. Do not expect big gains from the workspace by itself.

source: Goyal et al. (2022) shared workspace, bouncing balls slot-count sweep
finding: More workspace slots made specialist division of labour worse past a point. Best result was at a narrow but not tiny bottleneck.
limits: Non-monotone: 2 slots was worse than the baseline. One dataset (van Steenkiste 2018).
agent_relevance: Too tight a bottleneck hurts and too wide hurts. Tune the broadcast size; do not maximise it.

source: Goyal et al. (2022) shared workspace, Atari transfer
finding: RIMs plus shared workspace transferred better between Atari games than RIMs alone.
numbers: 36 game pairs. Ratio vs RIMs: game A median 1.13 (mean 1.16); game B median 1.11 (mean 1.15). 10 specialists; 10M steps on source, 10M on target.
limits: Authors credit forward transfer and less backward interference. No significance test in the text read. Compared only to RIMs.
agent_relevance: A shared state may cut interference between tasks. Test with held-out task switches.

source: Chateau-Laurent & VanRullen (2025) Learning to chain operations by routing information through a global workspace
finding: A GWT-style model with a learned router chains an incrementer to add two digits. Workspace has 10 dimensions. An LSTM router gates which module reads or writes each step.
numbers: One-hot version: test accuracy 100% on all (left, right) addend combos in the test set. MNIST-image version: 90.0%. Router trained 10,000 epochs, other parts frozen. Loss over T=20 steps rewards answering in few steps.
limits: Toy arithmetic. The MNIST router keeps incrementing after answering. The abstract says it beats LSTM and Transformer baselines on unseen addends; baseline numbers were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Closest to our design: a controller gates which module touches the workspace each step and chains steps. In our agent code, not a learned model, should do the routing.

source: Devillers et al. (2024) Semi-supervised multimodal representation learning through a global workspace
finding: A workspace that translates between vision and language latents works with few paired examples when cycle-consistency losses are added.
numbers: Semi-supervised GW needed about 4 to 7 times fewer paired examples than fully supervised to reach the same translation accuracy. ImageNet linear probe from visual GW: contrastive loss only 50.3 +/- 0.2% vs full GW 55.7 +/- 0.2%. COCO retrieval used 20% of train+restval as paired data.
limits: Two toy datasets plus COCO. The image-text bijection helps; it worked less well on natural language than on proto-language.
agent_relevance: A shared translation space lets one module's output be read by all. In a text scaffold, a common plain-text format plays this role.

source: VanRullen & Kanai (2021) Deep learning and the global workspace theory
finding: Opinion paper proposing a global latent workspace made by unsupervised translation between the latent spaces of modality-specific networks. Lists functional advantages of broadcast.
numbers: No experiments. Roadmap only.
limits: Position paper. Devillers 2024 and Chateau-Laurent 2025 supply the first tests.
agent_relevance: The workspace needs a translation layer so every module can read what is broadcast.

source: Dossa et al. (2024) Design and evaluation of a global workspace agent embodied in a realistic multimodal environment
finding: GW agent vs GRU agent on audiovisual navigation (SoundSpaces/SAVi). GW is steadier at small working-memory sizes. The gap fades when memory is large.
numbers: GW about 80% success at memory sizes 32,64,128,256,512 except 256 (some poor runs); GRU over 60%; random policy 0%; original SAVi RL agent 25%. 5 seeds, 150 eval trajectories, 56 training scenes, 21 target classes. Behavioural cloning on 500,000 oracle samples.
limits: Exact values only in a figure not read. No hypothesis tests. Authors say SAVi is not an adequate working-memory benchmark. Single task family. About 5 days per run on an RTX 3090.
agent_relevance: A workspace benefit shows mainly under tight capacity. Supports keeping our workspace small on purpose.

source: Butlin et al. (2023) Consciousness in artificial intelligence: insights from the science of consciousness
finding: Turns GWT into four indicators: GWT-1 parallel specialised modules; GWT-2 limited-capacity workspace with bottleneck and competition; GWT-3 global broadcast to all modules; GWT-4 state-dependent attention that queries modules in succession.
numbers: Four indicators. The authors say they build on one another and are not individually sufficient.
quote: only a relatively weak case that Transformer-based large language models possess any of the GWT-derived indicator properties
limits: Functional checklist, not a test of experience.
agent_relevance: The four indicators give a design spec for a code-held workspace: modules, a size cap, broadcast to all, state-dependent selection.

source: Butlin et al. (2023) on Transformers and the residual stream
finding: The residual stream could be called a workspace (lower dimension than layer widths, readable by later heads). Authors reject it: no recurrence, no single distinct workspace, bottleneck unclear.
numbers: Authors note the residual stream has the same dimensionality as the input to the system, so it is not clearly a bottleneck.
limits: Philosophical argument. The 2026 J-space paper tests an interpretability version.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM forward pass is not a workspace loop. A loop with an external state is closer.

source: Butlin et al. (2023) on Perceiver and Perceiver IO
finding: Perceiver has a single limited-capacity latent and state-dependent cross-attention, so it meets GWT-2 and part of GWT-4 but lacks broadcast.
numbers: Perceiver arguably has GWT-1, GWT-2 and the first part of GWT-4. Only one output module acts on the workspace per trial, set by an output query.
limits: Rated 'some way from being a full implementation of GWT'. Perceiver must be reset for a new task.
agent_relevance: Workspace-like designs help function but lack broadcast back to inputs. A code loop can add the broadcast step.

source: Butlin et al. (2023) design sketch for a GWT-satisfying AI
finding: Sketch: modules supply keys, workspace state gives a query, normalised similarity sets competition. Workspace state feeds top-down to all modules. An unrolled loop lets it recruit modules in succession.
numbers: A leaky integrator with a slow timescale is suggested to mimic sustained, ignition-like broadcast.
limits: Only a sketch; no test. Authors say recurrent sustaining may not be essential.
agent_relevance: Hold a chosen item for several steps unless displaced; a cheap copy of sustained broadcast.

source: Goldstein & Kirk-Giannini (2024) A case for AI consciousness: language agents and global workspace theory
finding: Argue that if GWT is true, language agents like Park et al. (2023) could easily be made conscious. Four conditions: parallel modules, competitive bottleneck, broadcast, workspace processing.
numbers: No numbers. They judge Park et al. agents not plausibly conscious as built. The fixes (a central workspace, three input modules, a competition function) are called no harder to build than the original.
limits: Conditional on GWT. No empirical test.
agent_relevance: The community already reads LLM agent loops as workspace candidates. Competition and capacity limit are the missing pieces.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) Theater of Mind for LLMs: a cognitive architecture based on global workspace theory
finding: Proposes Global Workspace Agents. An engine runs a Cognitive Tick: perceive and retrieve, think, arbitrate, update. Roles: attention agent, generator, critic (scores -5 to +5), meta agent, response agent.
numbers: No experiments or benchmarks. Generator temperature rises when thought diversity is low: Tgen = Tbase + alpha*exp(-beta*H(W)). Parameters unspecified.
limits: Pure design paper. Claims it breaks homogeneous-loop deadlocks, untested. Relies on LLM critic and meta agent to arbitrate, which our guardrail G5 warns against.
agent_relevance: Design contrast: our arbitration should be code, not a model meta agent. Entropy-driven exploration is a candidate trigger but needs a test.

source: Anthropic interpretability team (2026) Verbalizable representations form a global workspace in language models: J-space definition
finding: Defines a J-space with a Jacobian lens: representations the model is poised to verbalize. The workspace band spans about layer 38 to 92 percent of depth.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.5 main; Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5 corroborate. Lens averaged over about 1,000 prompts. Sparsity k at most 25. J-space is never more than 10% of an activation's variance (median 6 to 7% for concept vectors).
limits: Authors do not claim the full GWT architecture; broadcast happens in one forward pass, not by recurrence. Single-token vocabulary only. Read about 200k of 336k characters.
agent_relevance: A small verbalizable core exists inside the model and steers output. An external visible workspace is the text-level analogue we can control.

source: Anthropic interpretability team (2026) J-space causal swaps
finding: Swapping J-lens coordinates changes what the model reports and how it reasons.
numbers: Verbal-report swaps k=16: J-space component puts target in top-5 on 59% of trials vs 88% for pure lens vectors vs 5% for the non-J component. Multi-hop swaps, 50 prompts: 54% Haiku 4.5, 70% Sonnet 4.5, 70% Opus 4.5. Probe flip (n=90): J component flips answer 61% vs 28% for the rest, 6% when J-space clamped. Flexible swaps 76/192 top-1, 101/192 at alpha 2. Line-count task n=11: 46 became 65.
limits: Small n in several tests. Vocabulary restriction.
agent_relevance: A small readable core steers behaviour, so the contents of our workspace should be what we want steering the next step.

source: Anthropic interpretability team (2026) J-space capacity limits and intermediate steps
finding: The model's internal workspace is capacity limited and holds intermediate results in order.
numbers: J-space occupancy plateaus near 25 items (median) across workspace layers. Unrelated word lists: about six words present at a comma; 1 to 2 at a single layer. Arithmetic (4 + 17) * 2 + 7: 21, 42, 49 surface in order; 21 hits rank 1 near layer 71, 42 about 8 layers later.
limits: Multi-step arithmetic in J-space competes with holding another concept. Category switches clear the old category within a few words. Claude models only.
agent_relevance: Real LLMs show capacity limits and interference. Offload intermediate values to an external store.

source: Anthropic interpretability team (2026) J-space broadcast heads and ignition tests
finding: Finds attention heads that spread J-space content, and a sharp transition for choices.
numbers: Ablating the top 1% of broadcast heads: J-lens recall@25 falls to 0.67 vs 0.86 for random heads; injected-thought report rate falls 0.54 to 0.09 with control intact. MLP gain on J-lens vectors about 1 before the band and about 10x through it. Ignition test: 16 country pairs x 40 sentences, choice sharpens near layer 38.
limits: Bimodal response on ambiguous prompts, stronger in J-space. Ignition is suggestive, not shown to match brain ignition.
agent_relevance: Broadcast has a measurable mechanism in LLMs; a candidate target for monitoring.

source: Anthropic interpretability team (2026) counterfactual reflection training
finding: Fine-tuning Haiku 4.5 to write a values reflection when interrupted mid-rollout makes it more honest in uninterrupted rollouts, via J-space content.
numbers: 10,000 task prompts with partial rollouts. Fabrication benchmark (27 transcripts) 0.25 to 0.07. Deception benchmark (100 scenarios) 0.38 to 0.05. Ablating implanted J-space vectors: fabrication 0.07 back to 0.22 (176 vectors); deception 0.05 to 0.23 (63 vectors); base model fabrication stays 0.25, base deception 0.38 to 0.48.
limits: Fine-tuning, not a scaffold. Small benchmarks; the developer's own models and scoring.
agent_relevance: A reflection step can be carried into the core. For us a reflection step must be triggered by a signal (G1) and cite real output (G2).

source: Juliani, Arulkumaran, Sasai & Kanai (2022) On the link between conscious function and general intelligence in humans and machines
finding: Compares GWT, information generation theory and attention schema theory. All three tie conscious function to some part of domain-general intelligence. Proposes mental time travel as a joint target.
numbers: No experiments (abstract page read).
limits: Only the abstract page was read, so the GWT section details are unverified.
agent_relevance: Gives a link from broadcast to flexible general problem solving, but no measured gain.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior
finding: An agent loop with memory stream, retrieval, reflection and planning. A retrieval step picks which few memories enter the prompt, a workspace-like selection.
numbers: 100 Prolific raters ranked 5 conditions on believability. TrueSkill: full 29.89 (sd 0.72); no reflection 26.88 (0.69); no reflection or planning 25.64 (0.68); human crowdworkers 22.95 (0.69); no memory, planning or reflection 21.21 (0.70). Full vs prior-work baseline d=8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001. Dunn tests: all pairs significant except crowdworker vs fully ablated.
limits: Believability judged by raters, not task accuracy. Several components removed at once.
agent_relevance: Selecting memory into a small prompt plus reflection raised rated quality. Goldstein & Kirk-Giannini treat this as a near-workspace.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan & Griffiths (2023) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames a language agent as working memory plus long-term memories (episodic, semantic, procedural) and a decision loop. Working memory persists across LLM calls and each call's input is built from a subset of it.
numbers: No numbers. Maps Soar-style production systems onto LLM agents.
quote: a data structure that persists across LLM calls
limits: Conceptual; no benchmark.
agent_relevance: Matches our plan: code holds working memory, the model sees a built slice per call. Soar and ACT-R are older systems sharing this idea.

source: Butlin et al. (2023) on classical GWT-inspired software agents
finding: Cites Franklin & Graesser (1999) and Shanahan as earlier implementations of workspace ideas in artificial systems.
numbers: Reference mention only; no numbers from those systems were read.
limits: LIDA and Shanahan primary papers not opened here.
agent_relevance: Older LIDA-type systems exist; a gap to read in a later pass.

source: Dossa et al. (2024) probing results
finding: Linear probes read task facts out of the sensory features of the agents.
numbers: Target category from visual features 14 to 37% vs chance about 4% (1 of 21). Scene from visual features lowest 4% vs chance 1.79% (1 of 56); scene from audio 6 to 14%. Target probe accuracy falls once the sound stops.
limits: Values from text only; per-size values were in figures.
agent_relevance: Information in a workspace decays when input stops; needs a refresh or a store.

source: Park et al. (2023) limits
finding: Authors report that agents remember but embellish, and show failure modes.
numbers: Section 6.5.2 title: Generative Agents Remember, but With Embellishments.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: A memory item broadcast to all steps can be wrong; retrieved content needs checking against real output.

source: Goldstein & Kirk-Giannini (2024) objections
finding: Raise the point that a tiny functional system could meet GWT conditions, and that GWT was built for use within one brain.
numbers: No numbers. They reply that smallness is implausible for consciousness but applies to most functional theories.
limits: Philosophical.
agent_relevance: A cheap loop can imitate the structure. Structure alone does not show a better thinking result; that needs a benchmark.
